title: Walk Before Me and Be Blameless — a New Name, a Sign, a Laugh
blocks: Brothers and sisters, peace to you. Last time we came to a stop beside a well out in the wilderness, where a slave-woman who had been thrown away gave God a name and said: you are the God who sees me. And the last verse of that chapter tells us that Abram was eighty-six years old when Ishmael was born.
The first verse of today's chapter says, "When Abram was ninety-nine years old."

Brothers and sisters, thirteen years lie in that gap. Thirteen years, and the Bible does not record a single word of them. No vision. No promise. Not one "Yahweh said to Abram." What came of a man arranging matters for himself was a very long stretch of quiet.

And the question this lesson puts to us is the first sentence God spoke when he broke that silence: "Walk before me and be blameless." Did that sentence frighten you? Blameless — it sounds as though you may never put a foot wrong. Who on earth could manage that?

Let me put the answer up front: blameless does not mean spotless. It means handed over whole. And when God said it, the man standing in front of him was ninety-nine years old and had been living inside thirteen years of silence.
Verse 1: "When Abram was ninety-nine years old, Yahweh appeared to Abram and said to him, 'I am God Almighty.'"
"God Almighty" is אֵל שַׁדַּי (*El Shaddai*) — and this is the first time that name for God appears anywhere in the Bible.

Brothers and sisters, notice when that name arrives. God did not say "I am God Almighty" back when Abram was seventy-five, still strong in body, still with a little something to hope for. He introduces himself by that name at ninety-nine, with Sarai at eighty-nine, when the thing is biologically out of the question altogether.

Scholars take the etymology of the name several ways. Some connect it to the word for "mountain" — the One who stands on the height and cannot be shaken. Some break it up as "the One who is enough." But what deserves more attention is how the name is actually used inside Genesis: 17:2, 28:3, 35:11, 48:3 — nearly every time it appears, a line follows about being made fruitful and multiplied.
So inside Genesis, אֵל שַׁדַּי is "the God who can make the impossible bear fruit."

Brothers and sisters, this is a great comfort to us and a great challenge at the same time. The comfort is this: God does not say "I am the Almighty" while you still have options; he says it when your options have run out entirely. The challenge is this: if you still have a little something up your sleeve, perhaps you cannot yet hear that name at all.
God was silent for thirteen years. What was he doing in the meantime?

The text does not say, and that in itself is an honest answer. All we can see is the timeline: chapter 16 has him at eighty-six when Ishmael was born, and chapter 17 opens at ninety-nine. Thirteen years in between, and Scripture records not one sentence of them. For a great many people that is a comfort — there is a long blank page in the Bible too, and God did not leave because of it. What we must be careful about is inventing a story for those thirteen years, saying that God was disciplining him or training him. The text does not say it, so we do not say it. What we can say is this: when God spoke again, the first thing out of his mouth was "I am God Almighty." He did not reopen the old account. He reintroduced himself first.
What is so special about the name "God Almighty" (El Shaddai)?

The timing of אֵל שַׁדַּי (*El Shaddai*) in Genesis is telling: it mostly turns up when a person has run out of road, or when the promise looks impossible. There are several proposals about the root — one links it to "mountain" (the God who is like a mountain), one to "sufficiency" (the God who is all-sufficient), one to nursing and nourishing. Scholars have not settled the question, and we need not settle it for them. What is certain is how the name is used in its situation: a ninety-nine-year-old man is told he is going to have a son, and it is precisely then that God introduces himself as El Shaddai. So what the name is saying is this — when human possibility has dropped to zero, that is when the name is finally understood.
2. A Light from the Original: "Blameless" Is a Word from the Altar
The second half of verse 1: "Walk before me and be blameless."
Brothers and sisters, this sentence has to be explained properly, or it will crush a great many people.

The Hebrew behind "blameless" is תָּמִים (*tamim*). The word turns up most often in Leviticus, where it describes the animal brought for sacrifice: "he shall offer a male without defect" — and that phrase, "without defect", is *tamim*.
So the core of the word is not "morally without a single flaw." It is "whole, nothing chipped off, the entire animal present."
If a lamb is *tamim*, what that means is: the whole of it was given, and not one leg was held back.

So God is not saying, "You must get through life without ever making a mistake." He is saying: the whole of you is to be given over to me, and you are not to keep back one patch of ground that you still run yourself.

Brothers and sisters, in one stroke that changes the question entirely. The old question was, "Am I good enough?" The new question is, "Am I keeping a piece back?" And that second question — that one you can actually answer.

Every one of us has a locked room somewhere inside. It might be money. It might be a relationship. It might be an addiction. It might be a person you have no intention of forgiving. It might be your career plan. You can be thoroughly devout in every other room of the house — it is just that one room you will not discuss.

And notice the first half of that sentence: "Walk before me" — הִתְהַלֵּךְ לְפָנַי (*hithalech lefanai*), "to walk back and forth in my presence." You know this stem already: it is the one behind Enoch, who "walked with God" in 5:24, and Noah, who "walked with God" in 6:9.
So the full sense is this: walk in front of me, with the whole of you there. It is not a question of how fast you walk. It is that when you walk, all of you is present.
"Be blameless" — how could I possibly be blameless? Doesn't a demand like that crush a person?

The Hebrew תָּמִים (*tamim*) means "whole, with nothing missing", and Leviticus uses it of the animal brought for sacrifice — no broken leg, no blind eye, the whole beast. So it is not speaking of moral spotlessness; it is speaking of not keeping a piece back for yourself. And watch the context: the sentence in front of it is "I am God Almighty", and the sentence after it is "I will make my covenant between me and you." The order runs like this — first the Almighty God, and only then the blameless man; first the covenant, and only then the requirement. That is the crucial point: this is not a report card, it is an invitation into a relationship. And so the practical question is not "am I good enough?" but "which piece have I still not handed over?"
3. The New Name: Identity First, Experience Afterwards
Verse 5: "Your name will no more be called Abram, but your name will be Abraham; for I have made you the father of a multitude of nations."

"Abram", אַבְרָם, means "exalted father"; "Abraham", אַבְרָהָם, runs straight on into the phrase that follows it, "father of a multitude of nations", אַב הֲמוֹן גּוֹיִם. And that word הָמוֹן is a fascinating one. It does not simply mean "many" — it carries the sense of a roaring crowd, the sound of a great throng of people standing there.
And the difference between the two names, in Hebrew, is one extra letter set into the middle: ה — which is a letter out of God's own name.

Brothers and sisters, picture the scene for a moment. On this particular day a ninety-nine-year-old man, with one son born to a slave-woman and no other, walks back into the tent and announces to the whole household: from today, please call me "father of a multitude of nations."
Everybody in that household knew he had no son by his wife. So every single time somebody called him by name, they were announcing a thing that had not yet happened.

This is the Bible's consistent order: identity first, experience afterwards. God did not wait until a crowd of descendants had arrived before renaming him. He renamed him first, and then had him live with that name for fourteen years — Isaac would not be born until Abraham was a hundred.

And in verse 15 God renames Sarai too: "As for Sarai your wife, you shall not call her name Sarai, but her name shall be Sarah." In the whole Bible this is the only married couple God renames together. She is not a supporting character; she is inside the covenant as well. And God says immediately afterwards, "Kings of peoples will come from her."

Brothers and sisters, notice the background to all this. Abraham has only just acquired Ishmael in chapter 16, and in verse 18 here he is still saying to God, "Oh that Ishmael might live before you!" God's answer names a name: no — Sarah. The woman who had already given up, the woman whose bright idea had rebounded on her own head — God with his own mouth puts the promise back on her.
Why does a change of name matter so much? What is the difference between Abram and Abraham?

Abram (אַבְרָם) means "exalted father"; Abraham (אַבְרָהָם) means "father of a multitude of nations." The difference is a single letter, ה (*he*) — and that is a letter out of God's own name. Which is to say: God put a letter of his own name into the man's name. And the most staggering thing about it is the timing. On the day he was renamed "father of a multitude of nations", he did not have one child. So every time he introduced himself, he was announcing something that had not yet happened. That is intensely practical for us: the identity God gives a person very often comes before the experience. You may not be living that way yet, but the identity has already been handed to you — and an identity slowly pulls a person towards itself.
Sarai becomes Sarah. What does that renaming mean?

Both names have to do with the word for "princess", and the difference between them is a fine one; commentators explain it in different ways. One reading is that Sarai is "my princess", belonging to one particular person, while Sarah is simply "princess", belonging to everyone. Read that way it answers exactly to Abraham's renaming — both move from inside one household out to all the nations. More important still is what God says in verse 16: "I will bless her, and moreover I will give you a son by her. Yes, I will bless her, and she will be a mother of nations." Until that moment Sarai's name had been attached to nothing but barrenness. When God renamed her, he was taking off the label that had been the deepest pain of her whole life.
4. The Sign, the Laughter, and That Same Day
From verse 10 onwards God gives a sign: "Every male among you shall be circumcised."
Brothers and sisters, why this sign? I think there are three reasons.

First, it is marked on the place where life is handed on. The heart of this covenant is offspring, so the sign is set exactly where the offspring are going to come from. And every generation has to receive it afresh for itself.

Second, it cannot be seen. This is not a plaque hung over the door, and it is not a ring worn on the hand. Other people cannot see it; it is between you and God alone. Brothers and sisters, the easiest kind of faith today is the outward kind — the meetings, the title, the testimony, the post online. This sign asks about the place where nobody can see: have you ever set a mark there?
Third, it hurts. There is no breezy way to get past this one. And verse 24 says that Abraham was ninety-nine years old when he was circumcised — not an infant, an old man.

Then verse 17 gives us the most human moment in the chapter: "Then Abraham fell on his face, and laughed, and said in his heart, 'Will a child be born to him who is one hundred years old? Will Sarah, who is ninety years old, give birth?'"
He laughed. And the text says he laughed having "fallen on his face" — which is the posture of worship. Flat on the ground in front of God, and at the very same moment finding the whole thing absurd.
Brothers and sisters, those two things can apparently happen at once: worship and sheer disbelief. And God did not rebuke him for it.

And the loveliest close in the whole chapter comes at verse 23: "Abraham took Ishmael his son, all who were born in his house, and all who were bought with his money: every male among the men of Abraham's house, and circumcised the flesh of their foreskin in the same day, as God had said to him."

"In the same day" — בְּעֶצֶם הַיּוֹם הַזֶּה, on that very day. Ninety-nine years old, and the moment the words were out he did it, without letting a single day go by. Brothers and sisters, obedience left over until tomorrow mostly never happens at all.
Why this particular sign for circumcision? Would some other sign not have done just as well?

There are several layers here worth noticing. First, it is cut into the body rather than hung on the outside — a mark that cannot be taken off and cannot be shown to anybody, which is exactly what stops it being used for display. Second, it falls on the organ by which life is handed on, and that points straight at the content of this covenant: offspring. Third, it is a sign that draws blood, in line with the thread of redemption that runs through the whole Bible. And the New Testament carries that thread onto the heart: Romans 2 says that "circumcision is that of the heart, in the spirit, not in the letter", and Colossians 2 says that in Christ we were "circumcised with a circumcision not made with hands." So a believer today does not need circumcision in the flesh — but the same question still has to be answered: is there a mark on me that belongs to God and is shown to no one?
5. Distortions You Must Be Able to Spot

The first is preaching "be blameless" as sinless perfectionism. We have seen it already: the core of תָּמִים is wholeness and total belonging, not moral spotlessness. Preach it as perfectionism and you leave the congregation two roads — despair, or pretending. And a church full of people pretending is the hardest church in the world to pastor.

The second is preaching circumcision as an outward regulation still to be kept today. Romans 2:29 says, "but he is a Jew who is one inwardly, and circumcision is that of the heart, in the spirit, not in the letter." Colossians 2:11 says that what we received was "a circumcision not made with hands." Fail to carry the line forward into the New Testament and the sign gets turned into a condition of salvation. As for using circumcision to argue for infant baptism, godly churches have long differed on that, and we deal with it separately on the map of disputed questions; what both sides agree on is this — a sign cannot stand in for a person's own faith.

The third is preaching the romance of the new name and never mentioning those thirteen years of silence. Chapter 16 ends at eighty-six; chapter 17 opens at ninety-nine; in between there is a blank. Skip over it and your congregation will conclude that God always answers quickly — and the people in the room who are still waiting will walk out more anxious than they came in.

The fourth is preaching Ishmael as the child God did not want. In verse 20 God says plainly, "As for Ishmael, I have heard you. Behold, I have blessed him, and will make him fruitful, and will multiply him exceedingly." And Abraham circumcised him that very day. What Ishmael received was an abundant blessing; it is only that the covenant runs down the line of Isaac. God short-changed neither child.

The fifth is preaching "an everlasting covenant" as though nothing a person did could ever cut him off. Verse 14 says it very plainly: "The uncircumcised male who is not circumcised in the flesh of his foreskin, that soul shall be cut off from his people. He has broken my covenant." The covenant holds for ever for the offspring of Abraham as a whole, but an individual can place himself outside it. Romans 9:6 says, "For they are not all Israel that are of Israel." Being born into a Christian family and sitting in the same seat every week is not the same thing as being inside the covenant.
6. Two Real Questions from a Chinese Setting

The first question: Chinese people care enormously about the name — standing, reputation, face, title. In this chapter God gives a man a new name. How is that different from the name we chase? Brothers and sisters, the difference lies in three things. First, the source. Our names are mostly earned, fought for, endured into existence; Abraham's name was given to him, and given at the moment when he was least qualified for it. Second, the timing. We wait until the achievement is in hand before we dare use the title; God gives the name first and the substance afterwards — Abraham carried the name "father of a multitude of nations" for fourteen years without one legitimate son in the house. Third, the direction. Our names are mostly so that we will be seen; his name was so that other people would be blessed. So a Chinese regard for the name does not have to be denied in itself. What has to change is those three things: who gives it, when it is given, and who it exists for.

The second question: the elders in my family say that joining the church means turning my back on my ancestors — and I can hardly announce a new name for myself the way Abraham did. What am I supposed to do? Brothers and sisters, let me be very concrete about this one. First, the Bible does not ask you to change your Chinese name, and it does not ask you to cut yourself off from your family. After Abraham was renamed, he still sent his servant back to his own kindred to find a wife for Isaac. Second, the real change of name happens on the inside. Revelation 2:17 says that the one who overcomes will be given a white stone, "and on the stone a new name written which no one knows but he who receives it." That is a name other people do not know, and you do. Third — and this is the most practical of all — what your elders need to see is not your new name but your new temper. A person whose temper improves after coming to faith, who is readier to serve his parents, who is more honest than he used to be, is more persuasive than any explanation you could offer. You do not have to win that argument. You only have to live that name.
"Identity first, experience afterwards" — so how do I live like that identity while I still cannot see any of it?

There are three very practical things to do. First, change what you call yourself: stop introducing yourself in the old way ("I'm just the sort of person who loses his temper easily") and use the words God gives instead. Second, do one thing that only somebody with that identity would do — however small it is. On the very day Abraham was renamed, he had his whole household circumcised; he caught the name with an action. Third, do it with somebody else: ask a spiritual companion to call you by the new name. And one caution — this is not self-hypnosis, because that name is not one you gave yourself, it is one God gave you. All you are doing is refusing to fight against it any longer.
7. Living 321 Out — Hand Over That Key
Brothers and sisters, let us bring this lesson back to the Three Foundations, the Two Core Values and the Goal of 321.

Jesus is my role model — twice in this chapter Abraham falls on his face, once in verse 3 and once in verse 17. And Matthew 26:39 tells us that in Gethsemane the Lord Jesus "fell on his face, and prayed." Brothers and sisters, here is my model: faced with the hardest thing of all, his posture was to go down onto the ground, not to stand up and argue.

The Bible is my standard — and the standard this chapter gives is not a rule but a definition: blameless equals belonging entire. If your standard is only a checklist of behaviour, you will circle for ever inside the question "how many have I managed?" But if the core of the standard is belonging, the question becomes "which piece have I still not given?" Those two questions will grow completely different lives.

The Holy Spirit is my guide — notice the way God broke thirteen years of silence. He did not explain those thirteen years. He simply said, "I am God Almighty." Sometimes guidance is not an answer to the question you have been carrying about the past; it is the gift of a name big enough to walk forward on.

Let Jesus be King — "Walk before me and be blameless." If blameless is defined as handing over the whole, then letting Jesus be King becomes something extremely concrete: that room you have kept locked all this time — hand over the key to that one as well. Brothers and sisters, we often give him the entire house and keep back a single drawer. And the drawer is precisely what God is asking for in this chapter.

Let Jesus receive all the glory — look at who the subject of this chapter is. I am God Almighty. I will make my covenant between me and you. I will make you exceedingly fruitful. I have made you the father of a multitude of nations. I will give to you the land. God says "I" more than a dozen times over. And Abraham does exactly two things: he falls on his face, and he does what he was told.

Establish God's system — circumcision is a mark cut into the body, unseen, set at the very source of life. Brothers and sisters, God's system is established out of the hidden places. So to establish God's system you have to begin where nobody can see: the thoughts you think when you are alone, the history on your phone, the tone of voice you use with your own family. A system that is very spiritual in public and carries no mark in the hidden place will not hold up for long.

And here I want to say something honest about 321 itself. We use the word selflessness a great deal, and the תָּמִים of this chapter gives it a more accurate shape: selflessness is not "making yourself small", it is "handing over the whole." The two look very alike, and they are not the same. People who make themselves small usually end up full of self-contempt, forever placating, never daring to hold an opinion; people who hand over the whole can actually be at ease, because they know they already belong to a Master. Brothers and sisters, if a person grows more selfless and steadily loses his own voice, that direction may well have gone crooked.
8. Four Kinds of Heart, One Sentence: "Be Blameless"
Brothers and sisters, the same sentence — "Walk before me and be blameless" — sounds utterly different falling into four different hearts.

The proud heart hears: "That one I have more or less managed." This heart reads "blameless" as a checklist to be ticked off, and then awards itself ninety marks out of a hundred. Brothers and sisters, notice who the sentence was spoken to — a man who had waited twenty-four years and had only just made a mess of everything by arranging it in human fashion. If you finish this chapter feeling that you are doing rather well, you have most likely not understood the word.

The fearful heart hears: "I am finished; I will never manage it." This heart starts to despair the instant the word "blameless" is spoken. To that heart I want to say: put the word back into its original meaning — whole. What God wants is not a lamb with no defects; it is a lamb that is all there. You may bring your defects along with you, so long as you bring the whole of yourself.

The ashamed heart hears: "With a past like mine, how could I ever be called blameless?" You may be carrying a history you cannot speak about. Brothers and sisters, look at verse 17 — the very man who had just been told "be blameless" laughed out loud on the spot, because he found what God said absurd. And God did not withdraw a word of it. Your past cannot cancel his announcement.

The wounded heart hears: "So what is it they want me to hand over this time?" You may have been asked to hand over a great deal already; you may even have had things taken from you in the name of "consecration" and "submission." Brothers and sisters, let me say this as clearly as I can: the one to whom things are handed over in this chapter is God, and nobody else. Anyone who asks you to hand over "the whole" to himself, to an organisation, or to a leader is not preaching this verse. The whole that God asks for is so that he may give the whole of himself to you — verse 7 says, "to be a God to you and to your offspring after you." That is the heart of this covenant.
9. This Week, a Few Things You Can Do

First, find the locked room. Sit quietly for ten minutes and ask God one question: Lord, which piece am I still keeping back? Write down the answer he puts into your heart. You do not have to deal with it straight away — own it first.
Second, practise "in the same day." If God reminds you of something you ought to do this week, do it within twenty-four hours. Obedience left over until tomorrow mostly never happens at all.

Third, set a mark somewhere nobody can see. It might be five quiet minutes every morning. It might be deleting an app. It might be one sentence you will stop saying. Circumcision was an unseen sign — set one of your own this week.

Fourth, speak once out of the new identity God has given you. Find a name Scripture calls you by — beloved, chosen, a child of God — and say it over yourself every morning this week. Abraham carried his name for fourteen years before he saw it come true.

Fifth, tell this lesson to one friend outside the church this week, in three sentences. There is a ninety-nine-year-old man in the Bible, and God said to him, "Walk before me and be blameless." That word "blameless" in the original is the word used of a sacrificial animal, and it means "all there, with nothing chipped off", not "has never put a foot wrong." So what God wants is not for me to become perfect; it is for the whole of me to belong to him, with no patch of ground kept back that I still run myself.
Brothers and sisters, let us declare together before God:
I declare that blameless does not mean I never put a foot wrong; it means the whole of me belongs to him, with no patch kept back that I still run myself.
I declare that I will hand over the key to that locked room as well.
I declare that my identity was given to me by God first, and that I will live carrying that name even while I still cannot see it.
I declare that obedience will not be left over until tomorrow; it will be today.
This week I am supposed to hand over a piece I have been keeping back — but I do not know what that piece is.

Find it with three questions. First: what is it that I am unwilling to let God touch? When a particular area comes to mind and you instinctively say, "not that one", that is usually it. Second: what is it that I dare not raise in prayer? Not out of shame, but because I am afraid he will really ask me to deal with it. Third: if God required me to hand over one thing today, which one am I most afraid he would name? And once you have found it, do not rush to hand the whole of it over at once. Do one concrete small thing first — say its name out loud in prayer, tell a companion about it, or do one thing that runs contrary to it. "Blameless" means the whole animal offered, but the offering can be made a step at a time.
Brothers and sisters, if only one picture from this lesson may remain, let it be a ninety-nine-year-old man who finished two things in a single day.
In the morning he fell on his face, heard God say "you will be the father of a multitude of nations", and then laughed out loud, thinking to himself: can a man of a hundred still have a child?
In the afternoon he picked up a knife and circumcised himself, and Ishmael, and every male in the household. The text says: "in the same day."
Brothers and sisters, in his heart he thought it absurd, and his hands did it anyway.

That is an enormous release for us. Obedience does not have to wait until you have thought the whole thing through. You can find something barely credible and do it all the same. Faith is not the elimination of every question; it is going ahead and acting while the questions are still there.
And please remember what God named that child: "Isaac", which means "he laughs." God wrote that laugh into the name of the son of promise.

Brothers and sisters, God did not delete their laughter; he rewrote it. To begin with it was a bitter laugh, the laugh of a thing found impossible. A year later Sarah held the child in her arms and said, "God has made me laugh. Everyone who hears will laugh with me." The same word, two entirely different sounds.

The focus is not on whether I am blameless enough, not on how much I have kept back, and not on whether I can hold my faith together today. The focus is on Jesus — he is the one who is truly *tamim*, the Lamb without defect who was offered whole. Not I, but Christ.
May God bless every one of us this week: to hand over that key, and to do it today and not leave it until tomorrow. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.

Leader's note: the Three Transformations are one road running downward. The first drives the point into the head, the second carries it from the head into the heart, the third carries it from the heart into the week. If time runs short, cover fewer questions rather than skipping the third — without reaching the third transformation, this lesson stops at a mindset and goes no further.

Priority markers: ★★★ = highest priority; if time is short, discuss at least this one in each transformation. ★★ = second priority. ★ = if time allows. The multiplication assignment marked [Must do] may not be dropped; it can be finished at home.
Transformation One | Internalise — until it becomes mindset (about 20 minutes)
Purpose: through discussion, to drive the point of this lesson home as a clear mindset.

1. ★★ The word behind "blameless" in the original means "the whole animal, with nothing missing", not "has never done anything wrong." How does that definition change the way this command sounds to you?
2. ★★★ When he was renamed "father of a multitude of nations", he did not yet have a single child. Why does God give the identity first and the experience afterwards?
3. ★ After thirteen years of silence, the first thing God said was "I am God Almighty", not a rebuke. What does that show you about the God we have?
4. ★★ Circumcision is a mark cut into the body and shown to nobody. What does that have to remind us about "spiritual marks"?
Leader's reminder: the aim of this section is that people can say it, not that they answer beautifully. If someone is speaking in fragments, help him tidy it up; do not finish his sentence for him.
Transformation Two | Digest — until it becomes life (about 35 minutes · the heart of this lesson)
Purpose: through seeing, listening, thinking, speaking and doing, to digest the mindset until it becomes life.

5. ★★★ The manuscript named four kinds of heart — proud (I am blameless enough as I am), fearful (is God going to ask me for that one thing?), ashamed (I am carrying an old label), wounded (somebody once used "you are not spiritual enough" to hold me down). Which are you most like? What experience made you that way?
6. ★★ Read aloud: "I am God Almighty. Walk before me and be blameless." Then tell the group: where does that sentence touch you?
7. ★★ Is there an old label that has stuck to you for a long time — one somebody else gave you, or one you stuck on yourself? When was it put there?
8. ★ Finish this in one sentence: "If God were to rename me today, what would I want him to call me?"
9. ★★ This week, which piece of "I would rather God did not touch that" are you going to hand over? Name the first concrete step you will take.

Leader's reminder: question seven will reach deep into how people see themselves. Do not deny anyone's feelings for him, and do not brush it aside with "you just need more faith." If someone speaks of long-standing self-rejection, follow up with him privately after the meeting and help him find the support he needs.
Transformation Three | Transform — until it becomes daily living (about 25 minutes)
Purpose: through discussing concrete application, to transform life into daily living.
10. ★★ Is there somebody in your own home with an old label stuck on him? How will you call him by a new word this week?
11. ★ The same question in another setting: at work or at school, how will you address the person everybody looks down on?
